summary: Requests moving STD 39, BBN Report 1822 describing how a host connects to an IMP, from Standard to Historic status. The interface was the original ARPANET host-to-switch specification and was no longer in use.

plainLanguage.summary: It says an old instruction booklet for a machine nobody uses should be put in the museum instead of kept on the active shelf.

subtitle: Retiring a 1970s ARPANET host-to-switch interface standard that is no longer in use.

tldr.problem: BBN Report 1822, describing the hardware interface between hosts and ARPANET switches (IMPs), was made an Internet Standard (STD 39) even though the interface was no longer in use after 1983.
tldr.mechanism: RFC 3109 requests that the IESG (Internet Engineering Steering Group) move STD 39 from Standard status to Historic status, retiring the STD 39 number. The document briefly explains the interface's role in ARPANET history and its obsolescence.
tldr.outcome: STD 39 was moved to Historic status, marking the formal retirement of the 1822 interface standard. This is a straightforward standards housekeeping RFC with no technical content.

today: RFC 3109 is Informational and moved STD 39 to Historic status in May 2001. BBN Report 1822 is now a historical document relevant only to understanding ARPANET prehistory.

sections.title: The ARPANET Host-IMP Interface
sections.content:
BBN Report 1822 specified the hardware interface between a host computer and an Interface Message Processor (IMP), the packet switches that made up the ARPANET. The specification had to handle hosts with arbitrary word lengths (8, 12, 16, 24, 36, 60 bits and others) because the 8-bit byte standard had not yet been adopted in 1968.

The 1822 interface was bit-serial and asynchronous. From a software perspective, it defined the link-layer access protocol for ARPANET. BBN Report 1822 was published in the 1960s by Bolt, Beranek, and Newman under ARPA contract and became a standard reference for ARPANET administrators.
sections.plainLanguage: A company invented the wires and plugs that connected old computers to the early Internet. They wrote a manual for it.

sections.title: Transition to TCP/IP and Retirement
sections.content:
In 1983, the US Department of Defense moved ARPANET to TCP/IP and split it into ARPANET (research) and MILNET (military production). The military mandated a byte-oriented, X.25-based interface for MILNET IMPs. However, the research ARPANET continued to use the 1822 interface under the new Internet protocol suite.

BBN Report 1822 was made an Internet Standard (STD 39) in 1983, even though it was never published as an RFC. By 2001, the ARPANET itself no longer existed and no host-IMP connections using 1822 remained in operation.
sections.plainLanguage: When computers switched to a new Internet system in 1983, the old interface kept working on the research network for a while. But by 2001, nobody was using it anymore.

sections.title: Moving to Historic Status
sections.content:
RFC 3109 formally requests that STD 39 be moved from Standard status to Historic status. Historic RFCs document protocols and technologies that are no longer in use but are preserved for historical reference. The document notes that "ARPANET technology and the BBN 1822 interface are no longer in use" and therefore the standard can be retired.

The RFC includes a brief security consideration: moving STD 39 to historic status has no known effect on Internet security. The STD number 39 is retired and will not be reused.
sections.plainLanguage: The Internet engineering committee officially says this old standard is done and moving it to the history section.

references.text: Bolt, Beranek, and Newman, "Specification for the Interconnection of a Host and an IMP", BBN Report 1822.
